hints: Imagine sorting playing cards in your hand: you pick up one card at a time and slide it into place among the cards you already hold. Can you do the same with nums?

Insertion sort keeps the left part of the array sorted. Each new element is shifted left past bigger elements until it finds its spot. With up to 2000 values this quadratic sort is fast enough; the built-in sort is O(n log n).

1. For i from 1 to n - 1, store key = nums[i].
  2. Set j = i - 1.
  3. While j >= 0 and nums[j] > key, move nums[j] to nums[j+1] and decrease j.
  4. Place key at nums[j+1].
  5. Return nums.

approaches.name: Insertion sort
approaches.idea: Grow a sorted prefix; insert each new element by shifting larger ones right.

approaches.name: Built-in sort
approaches.idea: Arrays.sort uses an O(n log n) algorithm and is what you would use in practice.

explain: For [5, 2, 9, 1, 5]: insert 2 before 5 → [2, 5, 9, 1, 5]; 9 stays; 1 shifts past 9, 5 and 2 → [1, 2, 5, 9, 5]; the last 5 shifts past 9 only → [1, 2, 5, 5, 9], which is returned. The invariant is that nums[0..i-1] is always sorted before step i. Using > (not >=) keeps equal values in their original order and avoids extra shifts. Values reach 109 in size, which still fits in int.
recognize: Plain 'return the values in sorted order' with small n → any simple sort works; practise insertion sort, then use the built-in.
javascript: function sortArray(nums) { return nums.slice().sort((x, y) => x - y); }
